claims.claim: A web request takes milliseconds (keep Python/Flask for the web part)
claims.measured: python-flask plaintext p50 35.55 ms, p99 51.40 ms; python-fastapi p50 7.46 ms, p99 15.50 ms
claims.why: Measured Python request latencies are single-digit to tens of milliseconds, so "milliseconds" is accurate.

claims.claim: At roughly 50 runs a day the web layer will never be the bottleneck
claims.measured: python-flask 1,732 req/s plaintext, 1,529 req/s single DB query; python-fastapi 7,442 req/s plaintext on 1 CPU
claims.why: Even the slowest Python setup handles over a thousand requests per second, which is many orders of magnitude above a few dozen jobs a day.

claims.claim: Running jobs inside Flask request handlers means a few concurrent users would tie up the server / block workers
claims.measured: python-flask I/O-wait test: 276 req/s with a 10 ms wait per request at 256 connections, p50 915 ms, which works out to about 3 requests in progress at once
claims.why: The sync Flask setup served only about 3 blocking requests at a time, so a few long-running jobs would occupy all its workers.

claims.claim: Rewriting the web part in Go, Rust or C++ gives no benefit here; the compute time stays the same
claims.about: Go / Rust / C++ web servers vs Python, for a NumPy simulation
claims.why: The benchmark measures web-server overhead, not 20–90 s NumPy simulation runs, so it cannot show whether the compute time would change.

claims.claim: The 20 to 90 seconds is spent in NumPy code, which already runs compiled C underneath
claims.why: The measurements include no NumPy or numeric-library workloads.

claims.claim: Celery is heavier than you need for this volume
claims.why: Celery and other job-queue frameworks were not benchmarked.
